content: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) encompass conditions such as autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise specified (PDD-NOS). Antipsychotic medications have been utilized to manage irritability associated with ASD. Aripiprazole, a third-generation atypical antipsychotic, is a relatively novel pharmacological agent with a distinct mechanism of action compared to other antipsychotics. This review serves as an update to a prior Cochrane review from 2011, which evaluated the safety and efficacy of aripiprazole in individuals with ASD. The objective of this review was to assess the safety and efficacy of aripiprazole as a pharmacological treatment for individuals diagnosed with ASD. A comprehensive search was conducted in October 2015 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, among others. The search included studies published from 1990 onwards, as this marked the year aripiprazole became available. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing oral aripiprazole at any dosage to placebo in individuals with ASD. Two independent reviewers collected, evaluated, and analyzed the data. Meta-analyses were performed for primary and secondary outcomes when feasible, and the GRADE approach was employed to assess the overall quality of the evidence. Three trials were included in this review. Two of these trials were part of the previous review, while one additional placebo-controlled discontinuation study was incorporated. Although the search encompassed all age groups, the included studies were limited to children and adolescents. The trials generally exhibited a low risk of bias, with the exception of one study that had incomplete outcome data. The overall quality of evidence for most outcomes was deemed moderate. Two RCTs, involving 316 children and adolescents with ASD, evaluated the effects of aripiprazole over an eight-week period. Meta-analysis revealed that aripiprazole led to a mean reduction of 6.17 points on the Aberrant Behavior Checklist (ABC) Irritability subscale (95% confidence interval [CI]: -9.07 to -3.26), a 7.93-point reduction on the ABC Hyperactivity subscale (95% CI: -10.98 to -4.88), and a 2.66-point reduction on the ABC Stereotypy subscale (95% CI: -3.55 to -1.77). These findings were based on moderate-quality evidence. However, aripiprazole was associated with notable side effects. Children and adolescents taking aripiprazole experienced a mean weight gain of 1.13 kg compared to placebo (95% CI: 0.71 to 1.54). Additionally, there was an increased risk of sedation (risk ratio [RR]: 4.28, 95% CI: 1.58 to 11.60) and tremor (RR: 10.26, 95% CI: 1.37 to 76.63). These findings were also supported by moderate-quality evidence. A randomized, placebo-controlled discontinuation study found that 35% of children and adolescents who continued aripiprazole treatment experienced a relapse in irritability symptoms, compared to 52% of those who were switched to placebo. This corresponded to a hazard ratio of 0.57 (95% CI: 0.28 to 1.12), though the evidence quality for this finding was low. All three trials included in this review were funded by Bristol-Myers Squibb and Otsuka Pharmaceutical Company, with editorial support provided by Ogilvy Healthworld Medical Education and Bristol-Myers Squibb. In conclusion, evidence from two RCTs suggests that aripiprazole may be effective as a short-term pharmacological intervention for certain behavioral symptoms of ASD in children and adolescents. Specifically, it appears to reduce irritability, hyperactivity, and stereotypic behaviors. However, clinicians must weigh these benefits against the potential for adverse effects, including weight gain, sedation, drooling, and tremor. A long-term placebo discontinuation study indicated that relapse rates were similar between those continuing aripiprazole and those switched to placebo, highlighting the need for periodic re-evaluation of aripiprazole use after stabilization of irritability symptoms. It is important to note that the studies included in this review utilized diagnostic criteria from the DSM-IV, which have since been updated with the release of the DSM-5 in 2013.
